title: How to get a disability parking placard or plates in New Jersey
dek: Who qualifies, which form to use, what it costs and where to send it. Plus the rules for temporary placards after surgery or an injury.
keyFacts: Permanent placards and wheelchair symbol plates are free from the NJ MVC
Apply with form SP-41, signed by a qualified medical practitioner
Permanent placards last 3 years; plates renew yearly, medical recertification every 3 years
Temporary placards: form SP-68, $4, issued by your town's police chief, good for 6 months
MVC Special Plate Unit questions: 609-292-6500
body:
A disability parking placard can make the difference between going to the pharmacy yourself and asking someone else to go. In New Jersey, permanent placards and wheelchair symbol plates cost nothing. The paperwork is short. The main job is getting the medical part signed and sending the right originals.

This guide covers who qualifies, how to apply for a permanent placard or plates, how temporary placards work, and the rules that keep you out of trouble once you have one.

Who qualifies in New Jersey?

The NJ Motor Vehicle Commission (MVC) lists six medical conditions. You need to meet at least one:

  • Loss of use of one or more limbs from paralysis, amputation or another permanent disability.
  • A severe, permanent disability that means you cannot walk without a brace, cane, crutch, another person, a prosthetic device, a wheelchair or another assistive device.
  • Lung disease at a set level of severity, or use of portable oxygen.
  • A heart condition classified as Class III or Class IV under American Heart Association standards.
  • A severe, permanent limit on walking from an arthritic, neurological or orthopedic condition, or being unable to walk 200 feet without stopping to rest.
  • Permanent sight impairment of both eyes, certified by the NJ Commission for the Blind. This one qualifies for a placard only, not plates.

You do not have to drive. A placard belongs to the person with the disability, and whoever is driving them can use it when they are in the car.

Who can sign the medical form?

The MVC accepts certification from a physician, podiatrist, licensed chiropractor, nurse practitioner or physician assistant. They must be licensed in New Jersey or a neighboring state. The certification has to be dated within 60 days of your application, so do not let the signed form sit in a drawer.

Placard, plates or both?

If you qualify, you can choose one set of wheelchair symbol plates, one placard, or one set of plates plus a placard.

PlacardWheelchair symbol plates
CostFreeFree
Works inAny car you are riding inOne registered vehicle
How long it lasts3 years, then recertifyRenewed yearly with your registration; medical recertification every 3 years
Best forPeople who ride with different family membersA household with one main car

Plates can be registered to the person with the disability or to one family member who drives them. The MVC does not issue these plates for vehicles owned or leased by a company or organization.

A placard is usually the more flexible choice. If your daughter drives you on Mondays and a neighbor drives you on Thursdays, the placard goes with you.

How do I apply for a permanent placard or plates?

  1. Get form SP-41. This is the Application for Vehicle License Plates and/or Placard for Persons with a Disability. It is on the MVC disability plates and placards page. The SP-41A checklist that goes with it helps you avoid delays. If you do not use a computer, call 609-292-6500 and ask for an application to be mailed.
  2. Have the medical section completed. Bring the form to your doctor or other qualified practitioner. Check that it is signed and dated.
  3. Gather originals. For plates, include a copy of your vehicle registration. If you do not have a New Jersey driver license or non-driver ID, you will need documents that meet the MVC's 6 Points of ID rule. The MVC says it accepts original documents only, not photocopies, for identity.
  4. Apply in person or by mail. Take it to a motor vehicle agency, or mail it to: New Jersey Motor Vehicle Commission, Special Plate Unit, 225 East State Street, PO Box 015, Trenton, NJ 08666-0015.
  5. Keep your ID card with the placard. You will receive a Person with a Disability Identification Card. It is not transferable.

If someone else is applying for you, the MVC wants a notarized letter of authorization from you or your power of attorney.

No license? A New Jersey non-driver ID makes this and many other errands easier. See our guide to getting a NJ non-driver ID.

How do temporary placards work?

A hip replacement, a broken ankle or a bad fall can make walking hard for a few months. That is what temporary placards are for.

  • Form: SP-68, Application for Temporary Placard, signed by your physician or medical practitioner.
  • Where: your municipal police department. The chief of police issues temporary placards, not the MVC.
  • Cost: $4, by check or money order payable to NJMVC. Cash is not accepted.
  • How long: six months, with one six-month renewal allowed.

Call your police department's non-emergency number first to ask about hours and what to bring. Ask your surgeon's office to fill out the SP-68 before the operation, so it is ready the day you come home.

What are the rules once I have one?

The rules are simple, and the MVC enforces them.

  • Park in a wheelchair symbol space only when the person with the disability is in the car.
  • That person must carry their Person with a Disability Identification Card as proof.
  • Do not lend the placard. A family member running errands alone cannot use it.
  • Misuse can lead to the immediate loss of the ID card, placard and plates.

Lying on the application is a crime in New Jersey. The MVC notes that a false statement on this application is a fourth-degree crime, with fines of up to $10,000 and up to 18 months in prison.

Veterans with a disability and Purple Heart recipients

New Jersey has a separate placard (form SP-47) for veterans with a disability and Purple Heart recipients. It lets the vehicle owner park at municipal meters without paying for up to 24 hours. You will need your DD-214 or DD-215 and your VA disability award letter or Purple Heart proof.

Renewing, replacing and giving it back

Renewing. Placards last three years. To recertify, send a new SP-41 with a fresh medical certification by mail or bring it to an agency. There is no fee. For plates, the registration renews every year as usual, and the medical part is redone every three years.

Lost or stolen. Replacements are free. If both the card and placard are lost, the MVC asks for a notarized statement or a signed letter completed in front of an MVC employee. A stolen placard also needs a police report.

When you no longer need it. If you stop qualifying, return the plates and ID card and apply for regular plates.

Get the medical form signed first, then send it within 60 days.

Where to get help

For MVC questions about plates and placards, call the Special Plate Unit line at 609-292-6500 (TTY 711). The NJ Division of Disability Services can point you to other help at 1-888-285-3036. For broader help getting around after you stop driving, see our guides to driving later in life and NJ Transit reduced fares.

faq.q: How much does a handicap placard cost in New Jersey?
faq.a: Permanent placards, wheelchair symbol plates, recertification and replacements are free. A temporary placard costs $4, paid by check or money order to NJMVC.

faq.q: Where do I get a temporary disability placard in NJ?
faq.a: From your municipal police department, not the MVC. Bring form SP-68 signed by your doctor or medical practitioner. It is good for six months and can be renewed once.

faq.q: How long is a New Jersey disability placard good for?
faq.a: A permanent placard is valid for three years. You recertify with a new SP-41 and a medical practitioner's certification.

faq.q: Can my son use my placard when I am not in the car?
faq.a: No. The placard can only be used when the person with the disability is in the vehicle and carrying their Person with a Disability Identification Card. Misuse can lead to losing the placard and plates.

faq.q: Who can sign the SP-41 medical certification?
faq.a: A physician, podiatrist, licensed chiropractor, nurse practitioner or physician assistant licensed in New Jersey or a neighboring state. It must be dated within 60 days of your application.

title: How to get NJ Transit reduced fares as a senior
dek: Riders 62 and older pay half the regular one-way fare on NJ Transit buses, trains and light rail. Here is what ID works, how to buy the ticket and when you need the Reduced Fare card.
keyFacts: Age 62+ rides NJ Transit bus, rail and light rail at 50% of the regular one-way fare
Any government-issued ID with your birth date works, including a Medicare card
Metro-North trips (Port Jervis Line) use a 65+ age rule
The free Reduced Fare ID now must have a photo; non-photo cards stopped working Jan 1, 2026
Access Link paratransit: 973-491-4224
body:
If you are 62 or older, NJ Transit cuts your one-way fare in half. That applies on buses, trains and light rail, at any time of day. You do not need to sign up for anything to start. You just need the right ticket and an ID that shows your birth date.

Here is how the discount works, what ID to carry, how to buy the ticket and when the Reduced Fare card is worth getting.

Who gets the senior fare?

  • Riders 62 and older. The discount is 50% of the regular one-way fare on NJ Transit bus, rail and light rail.
  • Riders with disabilities, at any age, through NJ Transit's Reduced Fare Program.
  • Metro-North trips. For travel to or from Metro-North stations, such as on the Port Jervis Line, the age is 65 and Metro-North's fare rules apply.

You do not have to live in New Jersey. NJ Transit says non-residents can use the Reduced Fare Program too, which helps when grandparents visit from out of state.

What ID do I need to show?

Seniors can use any ID or document that shows your date of birth and was issued by a government, social service agency or transit agency. NJ Transit lists these examples:

  • NJ Transit Reduced Fare ID
  • Medicare card
  • Driver license or state-issued non-driver ID
  • Passport or birth certificate
  • County, Medicaid or military ID
  • MTA Reduced Fare card, PATH Senior Fare card, or a Pennsylvania senior transit ID or PACE card

The Medicare card is the easy choice for most people. It fits in a wallet and you probably carry it already. If you gave up your license, a NJ non-driver ID also works.

For Metro-North trips, Metro-North's own fare rules apply, and it asks seniors 65 and older for proper identification. Call Metro-North at 212-532-4900 to check which IDs it accepts.

How do I buy a senior ticket?

On the NJ Transit app

Buy a reduced fare ticket in the NJ Transit Mobile App. Keep your ID handy, because a conductor or operator may ask to see it.

At a ticket machine

At a ticket vending machine, choose the Senior/Passenger with Disability ticket type before you pay.

At a ticket office, or on board

Show your ID to the ticket agent, bus operator, light rail operator or train conductor and pay the reduced fare.

Riding a private bus line?

Some interstate buses in New Jersey are run by private companies and are not marked NJ Transit. On those, NJ Transit says you also need a Reduced Fare Coupon for each ride. Ask the bus company before you travel.

The discount is on one-way fares. NJ Transit's pages do not describe a senior discount on monthly passes, so compare costs before buying a pass. If you ride only a few days a week, senior one-way tickets may cost less.

Should I get the Reduced Fare ID card?

Seniors do not need it, since a Medicare card or license works. But some people like having one card made for transit. The card is free, has your photo and is good for four years.

Important change: As of January 1, 2026, NJ Transit no longer accepts Reduced Fare ID cards without a photo. If you have an old card with no picture, apply for a new one or carry your Medicare card instead.

How to apply

  • Online at reducedfare.njtransit.com.
  • By mail. Print the application from the Reduced Fare Program page and mail it with proof of age and a recent photo to: NJ Transit, Reduced Fare Program, 2 Gateway, Suite 900, 283-299 Market St., Newark, NJ 07102.
  • In person. NJ Transit says seniors can apply at most local banks, savings and loan associations and county offices on aging. Bring your Social Security card and proof of age, such as a birth certificate or driver license.
  • Customer service offices at Newark Penn Station, New York Penn Station, Hoboken Terminal and the Port Authority Bus Terminal.

The card arrives by mail about four weeks after you apply. For help in another language with a reduced fare question, NJ Transit lists 973-491-7112.

Riders with a disability apply differently. A physician or certifying agency completes the application. If you need a personal care assistant, the physician can certify that, and the assistant then rides free with you.

What if I cannot use a regular bus?

Access Link is NJ Transit's paratransit service. It is a shared-ride, curb-to-curb service for people whose disability keeps them from using local buses or light rail. It runs in the same areas and hours as local bus routes.

  • To apply, call 973-491-4224 and choose option 1. You will have an interview by phone or in person and need current medical verification.
  • To book rides, call the same number. Next-day trips can be booked daily from 7:30 a.m. to 4 p.m., and trips further out from 7:30 a.m. to 3 p.m. You can also book online or in the Access Link app.
  • Fares are based on the local bus fare and the zones traveled. The Reduced Fare card does not apply on Access Link. Approved personal care attendants ride free.

Many counties also run their own senior and disability transportation for medical visits and shopping. To find yours, call the Aging and Disability Resource Connection at 1-877-222-3737.

Carry your Medicare card. It is all most seniors need for half-price fares.

Quick tips for a smoother trip

  • Plan off-peak trips if you can. Trains and buses are less crowded, and it is easier to get a seat.
  • Ask the conductor or bus operator for help if you need extra time to board.
  • Keep your ID in the same pocket as your phone or ticket so you are not hunting for it.
  • For general NJ Transit questions, the Information Center is 973-275-5555.

Looking for places to go? Our day trips guide and free and discounted list have ideas you can reach without a car.

faq.q: What age is the senior discount on NJ Transit?
faq.a: 62 and older. Seniors pay 50% of the regular one-way fare on NJ Transit buses, trains and light rail. For trips to or from Metro-North stations, the age is 65.

faq.q: Can I use my Medicare card for NJ Transit reduced fare?
faq.a: Yes. NJ Transit accepts a Medicare card as proof of age for the senior fare. You can also use a driver license, non-driver ID, passport or NJ Transit Reduced Fare ID.

faq.q: Do I need an NJ Transit Reduced Fare card as a senior?
faq.a: No. Any government-issued ID showing your birth date works. The Reduced Fare ID is free and optional, but older cards without a photo stopped being accepted on January 1, 2026.

faq.q: How do I buy a senior ticket at an NJ Transit machine?
faq.a: Choose the Senior/Passenger with Disability ticket type on the ticket vending machine. Carry your ID in case a conductor or operator asks to see it.

faq.q: Does the senior discount work on Access Link?
faq.a: No. Access Link fares are based on the local bus fare and zones, and Reduced Fare cards cannot be used. Approved personal care attendants ride free.

title: How to get a New Jersey non-driver ID
dek: Giving up the car keys does not mean giving up a photo ID. Here is what a NJ non-driver ID costs, what to bring to the MVC and how to make the switch easier.
keyFacts: Standard NJ non-driver ID: $24 (renewal $24, duplicate $11)
With a disability and form GU-12 signed by a physician: $6, no renewal fee
First card requires an in-person appointment at an MVC Licensing Center
Bring form BA-208, 6 Points of ID, proof of address and your Social Security number
REAL ID needs 2 proofs of address; MVC lists REAL IDs at $35
body:
Many people stop driving long before they stop needing ID. You still need a photo ID at the bank, the pharmacy counter, the doctor's office and the airport. In New Jersey, the answer is a non-driver ID from the Motor Vehicle Commission (MVC). It looks like a license, but it is only for identification.

This guide explains who can get one, what it costs, what to bring and how to plan the visit so you only make one trip.

Who can get a non-driver ID?

Any New Jersey resident 14 or older can apply. The card is for identification only and does not let you drive.

Two things to know:

  • If you still hold an out-of-state driver license, you are not eligible.
  • If your license is suspended, the MVC lets you downgrade to a non-driver ID until the suspension is resolved.

The MVC also notes that a non-driver ID cannot be used to park in disability spaces. That needs a separate placard. See our guide to NJ disability placards and plates.

What does it cost?

CardFee
Standard non-driver ID, first card$24
Renewal$24
Duplicate or lost card$11
Non-driver ID for a person with a disability, first card$6
Renewal for a person with a disabilityNo fee

The MVC does not list a separate senior discount. The lower fee is for people with a disability. To get it, a physician must complete the Physician Certification for Blind or Disabled Person form, called the GU-12. Bring it to your appointment.

The MVC takes cash, checks, money orders and major credit cards.

Standard ID or REAL ID?

Since May 7, 2025, you need a REAL ID or another accepted document, such as a valid passport, to board a domestic flight. The MVC says REAL ID is not mandatory, especially if you already have a valid passport.

  • Standard ID needs one proof of address.
  • REAL ID needs two proofs of address, your Social Security number and identity documents worth 6 REAL ID points. The point values differ from the standard card. The MVC lists REAL IDs at $35, compared with $24 for standard cards.

If you fly to see grandchildren and do not have a current passport, REAL ID is probably worth it. If you rarely fly, a standard card is fine. Both are available by appointment at MVC Licensing Centers.

What do I need to bring?

  1. Form BA-208. This is the application for a permit, license or non-driver ID. You can fill it out ahead of time.
  2. 6 Points of ID. Documents proving your age and identity that add up to 6 points. These must be paper originals. Use the document tool on the MVC 6 Points of ID page to check your mix before you go.
  3. Proof of New Jersey address. One for a standard card, two for REAL ID. The MVC accepts things like a bank statement, a utility or credit card bill, a W-2 or a current NJ registration. Paper or electronic copies are accepted for address.
  4. Your Social Security number.
  5. Form GU-12, if you are applying for the disability rate.
  6. Payment.

Documents not in English need a certified translation.

Name changed over the years?

If the name on your birth certificate does not match your current name, bring the papers that connect them, such as a marriage certificate or divorce decree. If you are unsure what counts, ask the MVC before your appointment.

How do I get the card?

Your first non-driver ID has to be done in person at an MVC Licensing Center, by appointment. Book through the MVC's online appointment system at telegov.njportal.com/njmvc.

At the appointment, staff check your documents and take your photo. The photo must show your full face, from the top of your forehead to the bottom of your chin. If you wear a head covering for medical or religious reasons, tell staff at the camera station.

Your new card is mailed to you. When it is time to renew, the MVC says you can do it online through MyMVC.

Book the appointment first. Then spend the waiting days gathering the right papers.

Renewing or replacing your card

A renewal costs $24, or nothing if you have the disability version. The MVC says renewals can be done online through MyMVC, so you may not need another trip.

A lost or damaged card costs $11 to replace. If your wallet was stolen, think about more than the ID. Call your bank, watch your accounts and see our guide to scams for next steps.

Keep a photocopy of the card, and of your Medicare card, in a safe place at home. It will not replace the real card, but it makes the replacement visit easier, because you will have your ID number and details handy.

Switching from a license to an ID

For a lot of families, this card is part of a bigger conversation about driving. A few ideas make the change easier:

  • Go together. An adult child can book the appointment, help gather papers and drive. Bring a folder with everything in order.
  • Plan new ways to get around. Riders 62 and older pay half fare on NJ Transit, and a non-driver ID works as proof of age. See our guide to NJ Transit senior fares.
  • Update your records. Let your bank, pharmacy and insurance companies know if your ID number changes.

If you are still deciding whether it is time to stop driving, our guide to driving later in life walks through warning signs and options.

Where to get help

The MVC website is the best place to check current fees and documents. If you need help with transportation to the appointment, call the Aging and Disability Resource Connection at 1-877-222-3737 to reach your county office on aging. For anything else, dial 2-1-1.

faq.q: How much is a non-driver ID in NJ?
faq.a: $24 for a standard card, $24 to renew and $11 for a duplicate. People with a disability pay $6 for the first card and nothing to renew, with form GU-12 signed by a physician.

faq.q: Do seniors get a discount on a NJ non-driver ID?
faq.a: The MVC does not list a senior discount. The reduced $6 fee is for people with a disability who bring a physician's GU-12 certification.

faq.q: Can I get a NJ non-driver ID online?
faq.a: Not the first one. Your first card must be done in person at an MVC Licensing Center by appointment. Renewals can be done online through MyMVC if you are eligible.

faq.q: What do I need to bring for a NJ non-driver ID?
faq.a: Form BA-208, documents worth 6 Points of ID, proof of your New Jersey address and your Social Security number. REAL ID needs two proofs of address instead of one.

faq.q: Can I fly with a NJ non-driver ID?
faq.a: Since May 7, 2025, you need a REAL ID or another accepted document, such as a valid passport, for domestic flights. Ask for the REAL ID version if you plan to fly without a passport.

title: How to report elder abuse or neglect in New Jersey
dek: Who to call depends on where the person lives. Here is a calm, step by step guide to reporting worries about an older adult at home, in a nursing home or in assisted living.
keyFacts: Danger right now: call 911
At home or in the community: county Adult Protective Services (statewide line 1-855-835-5277)
Nursing homes and assisted living: Long-Term Care Ombudsman, 1-877-582-6995
Licensed facility complaints, 24/7: NJ Department of Health, 1-800-792-9770
APS records and reports are confidential
body:
Maybe a neighbor has not been seen in days and the mail is piling up. Maybe your aunt's new "friend" is suddenly handling her bank account. Maybe your father has bruises he cannot explain after a stay in a care home. When something feels wrong, it is hard to know whether to speak up, and who to call.

In New Jersey, you do not have to be sure abuse is happening to make a report. You only need a real concern. Trained staff will look into it. This guide explains who handles what, what to say, and what happens next.

Is someone in danger right now?

If a person is hurt, being threatened, or in immediate danger, call 911. Do not wait to figure out which agency is the right one. Police and emergency crews can act right away, and they can bring in other agencies later.

Who should I call? It depends on where the person lives

Where the person livesWho to call
Their own home, a relative's home, or another community settingCounty Adult Protective Services (APS)
A nursing home, assisted living, residential health care facility or other long-term care settingNJ Long-Term Care Ombudsman, 1-877-582-6995
Care problems at any licensed health facility (hospital, nursing home, assisted living, home health agency, adult medical day care)NJ Department of Health complaint hotline, 1-800-792-9770, 24 hours a day
Medicare billing for care that was never givenNJ Senior Medicare Patrol, 1-732-777-1940 ext. 1117

If you are unsure, call any of these. Staff will tell you if someone else should take it, and you will not be in trouble for calling the "wrong" place.

Adult Protective Services: for people living in the community

Each county has an Adult Protective Services (APS) program. APS looks into reports of abuse, neglect and exploitation of vulnerable adults 18 and older who live in the community. That includes a private home or another setting that is not licensed or run by the state.

APS is for adults who may not be able to protect themselves because of illness or disability. It also handles self-neglect, such as a person living alone who has stopped eating, taking medicine or keeping the home safe.

Call the APS office in the county where the person lives. The statewide line, run by the NJ Division of Aging Services, is 1-855-835-5277 (1-855-TELL-APS).

What APS can and cannot do

APS staff meet with the person, assess what they need and recommend services. The goal is to stabilize the situation in the least intrusive way while respecting the person's right to make their own choices.

The state is clear about limits. APS cannot remove someone from their home without a court order. It cannot force services on an adult who has the capacity to decide. It cannot move a person to another living situation without their agreement or a legal representative's. That can feel frustrating to families. It also means an older adult keeps their rights.

Long-Term Care Ombudsman: for nursing homes and assisted living

The New Jersey Long-Term Care Ombudsman is an independent state office that advocates for residents of nursing homes, assisted living and other long-term care settings. It investigates allegations of abuse, neglect and exploitation.

  • Phone: 1-877-582-6995. The state's resident rights poster describes the line as confidential and says callers may remain anonymous.
  • Email: ombudsman@ltco.nj.gov
  • Online: the Ombudsman complaint form
  • Mail: NJ Long-Term Care Ombudsman, P.O. Box 852, Trenton, NJ 08625-0852

The Ombudsman also helps with problems that are not abuse, such as a sudden discharge notice or a dispute over care. In New Jersey assisted living, residents have the right to written notice at least 30 days before a facility-requested transfer or discharge, and the notice must name the Ombudsman.

What should I say when I call?

You do not need proof. Share what you know firsthand. The state asks for as much of this as you have:

  • The person's name, address and phone number
  • Their date of birth, if you know it
  • Any health or memory problems you know about
  • Family members, helpers or agencies involved
  • What you saw or heard, when, and who was involved

Write a few notes before you call. Dates, times and exact words help. If you are reporting about a facility, include the name of the facility and the staff involved, if you know them.

Is my report confidential?

The state says all APS records and communications about reports, evaluations and services are confidential. Information can be shared only when a court orders it or when APS needs it to do its legal duties.

Signs that something may be wrong

Abuse can be physical, emotional, sexual or financial. Neglect can come from a caregiver or from the person themselves. Some signs families notice:

  • Injuries that are not explained, or explanations that change
  • Sudden fear, withdrawal or confusion around a certain person
  • A caregiver who will not let you visit alone
  • Missing money, new names on accounts, or bills going unpaid
  • Weight loss, poor hygiene, or a home that has become unsafe

Money problems are common. If you suspect a scam or someone taking advantage, our guide to scams explains how to protect accounts. Talking with the person's bank can also help.

You do not need proof to call. You need a real concern.

After you report

Expect a call back with questions. You may not hear the outcome, because of confidentiality. That is normal. If the situation gets worse, call again, and call 911 in an emergency.

Caring for someone who is being hurt or exploited is stressful. If you are a family caregiver feeling stretched, see our guides to respite care and starting the conversation about care. For local services of any kind, call the Aging and Disability Resource Connection at 1-877-222-3737 or dial 2-1-1.

faq.q: How do I report elder abuse in New Jersey?
faq.a: If someone is in danger, call 911. For an adult living at home, call the county Adult Protective Services office or the statewide line, 1-855-835-5277. For a nursing home or assisted living resident, call the Long-Term Care Ombudsman at 1-877-582-6995.

faq.q: Can I report elder abuse anonymously in NJ?
faq.a: The state's resident rights poster says callers to the Long-Term Care Ombudsman may remain anonymous. APS records and reports are confidential and shared only by court order or when APS needs them to do its job.

faq.q: Who investigates abuse in New Jersey nursing homes?
faq.a: The NJ Long-Term Care Ombudsman investigates abuse, neglect and exploitation of residents. The NJ Department of Health also takes complaints about licensed facilities 24 hours a day at 1-800-792-9770.

faq.q: Can Adult Protective Services remove someone from their home?
faq.a: Not without a court order. APS also cannot force services on an adult who has capacity to decide, or move them without their agreement or a legal representative's.

faq.q: What is self-neglect?
faq.a: Self-neglect is when a vulnerable adult can no longer meet their own basic needs, such as food, medicine or a safe home. In New Jersey, county APS programs handle reports of self-neglect for adults living in the community.

title: Free tax help for seniors in NJ: AARP Tax-Aide and VITA
dek: Trained volunteers prepare federal and New Jersey returns for free every winter. Here is who qualifies, how to find a site when they open and what to bring.
keyFacts: AARP Foundation Tax-Aide is free; you do not need to be an AARP member
Tax-Aide appointments run from early February to mid-April
Find Tax-Aide sites: 1-888-227-7669 (locator reopens each tax season)
Find IRS VITA and TCE sites: 1-800-906-9887
NJ does not tax Social Security benefits
body:
Paying someone to do a simple tax return can cost more than a week of groceries. In New Jersey, you may not have to. Two volunteer programs prepare federal and New Jersey returns for free, and most returns are filed electronically.

The catch is timing. Sites are set up each winter and the lists go live when tax season starts. This guide tells you what to expect, how to find a site and what to bring so you get it done in one visit.

What are the free programs?

AARP Foundation Tax-Aide

AARP Foundation Tax-Aide is free tax preparation by IRS-certified volunteers. It focuses on people over 50 with low to moderate income. You do not need to be an AARP member. You can have a volunteer prepare and file your return, or get coaching to do it yourself. Sites are often at libraries, senior centers, banks and community centers.

VITA and TCE

The IRS runs two volunteer programs through local partners:

  • VITA (Volunteer Income Tax Assistance) helps people with low to moderate income, people with disabilities and people who speak limited English. The IRS says many sites serve people who generally make about $70,244 or less, though each site can set its own limits.
  • TCE (Tax Counseling for the Elderly) is for people 60 and older and focuses on pensions and retirement questions. The IRS notes that most TCE sites are run by AARP Foundation Tax-Aide.

The NJ Division of Taxation says volunteers at both programs are trained to prepare federal and New Jersey returns.

When do sites open?

AARP says Tax-Aide appointments run from early February to mid-April. Sites and hours are announced each winter, and they change from year to year. Right now, in late fall, the AARP site locator is closed until the next tax season.

A good plan:

  • In January, check the locators below or call. Sign up for AARP Tax-Aide text alerts if you like reminders.
  • As soon as sites post, call or book an appointment.
  • Collect your forms as they arrive in January and February in one folder.

How do I find a site near me?

ProgramOnlinePhone
AARP Foundation Tax-AideAARP Tax-Aide site locator1-888-227-7669
IRS VITA and TCEIRS VITA/TCE locator1-800-906-9887

Your local library, senior center and county office on aging also hear about sites early. Call your library's reference desk in January and ask. You can reach your county office on aging through the Aging and Disability Resource Connection at 1-877-222-3737.

Some sites are listed as "Self-Prep." There, you prepare your own basic return with a volunteer available to help.

What should I bring?

This list comes from the IRS checklist for free tax preparation. Bring originals or copies of:

  1. Original photo ID for you, and your spouse if filing jointly.
  2. Social Security cards for you, your spouse and any dependents, plus birth dates.
  3. Income forms: SSA-1099 for Social Security, 1099-R for pensions and IRA withdrawals, W-2s, and 1099s for interest and dividends.
  4. Last year's federal and state returns, if you have them.
  5. Bank routing and account numbers for direct deposit, such as a blank check.
  6. Form 1095-A if you had Marketplace health insurance.

If you file jointly and e-file, the IRS says both spouses must be present to sign. Plan the visit for a day you can both go.

Keep a list of anything unusual

Did you sell a house, start withdrawals from an IRA, or have a spouse pass away this year? Write it down and bring any papers. Volunteers handle many situations, but services vary by site. If your return is complicated, call ahead and ask whether the site can help.

Want to do it yourself, or help others?

Tax-Aide offers two ways to get help. A volunteer can prepare and file your return, or you can get coaching and prepare it yourself. Some IRS sites are listed as "Self-Prep," where you do your own basic federal and state return with a volunteer nearby. Questions about Tax-Aide can go to taxaide@aarp.org.

If you are retired and good with numbers, think about volunteering. The NJ Division of Taxation has pages on becoming a VITA volunteer, becoming a TCE volunteer with AARP Tax-Aide, and opening a new site. Volunteers are trained and certified by the IRS every year. It is a useful way to stay sharp and help neighbors at the same time.

New Jersey tax points seniors ask about

  • Social Security is not taxed by New Jersey. The Division of Taxation lists Social Security and Railroad Retirement benefits as nontaxable.
  • Pension exclusion at 62. If you are 62 or older, or disabled under Social Security rules, you may be able to exclude pension and other retirement income. With total income of $100,000 or less, the maximum exclusion is $100,000 for married couples filing jointly, $75,000 for single filers and $50,000 for married filing separately. It phases down between $100,001 and $150,000 and ends above $150,000.
  • Military pensions are not taxed by New Jersey, at any age.

Volunteers are trained on New Jersey returns. It still helps to know about them so you can check your return.

Start looking in January, and keep every tax form in one folder as it arrives.

Other money help to pair with tax time

Tax season is a good moment to check other benefits. The state's property tax relief programs, ANCHOR, Senior Freeze and Stay NJ, have their own application. See our property tax relief guide for current deadlines. For drug costs and utility bills, see prescription and bill help and food and utility help.

Watch for scams, too. If a call, text or email claiming to be from the IRS demands payment, stop and check before you do anything. Our scams guide explains what to do.

faq.a: Yes. AARP Foundation Tax-Aide is free, and you do not need to be an AARP member. It focuses on people over 50 with low to moderate income.

faq.a: AARP says appointments run from early February to mid-April. Sites and dates are announced each winter, and the online site locator reopens for the new tax season.

faq.a: Use the AARP Tax-Aide locator or call 1-888-227-7669. For IRS VITA and TCE sites, use the IRS locator or call 1-800-906-9887. Libraries and senior centers also list local sites.

faq.a: Yes. The NJ Division of Taxation says volunteers at VITA and TCE sites are trained to prepare both federal and New Jersey returns.

faq.a: No. The NJ Division of Taxation lists Social Security and Railroad Retirement benefits as nontaxable retirement income.

faq.a: Photo ID, Social Security cards, all income forms such as SSA-1099 and 1099-R, last year's returns and bank details for direct deposit. Both spouses must be present to sign an e-filed joint return.

title: Staying safe in a New Jersey heat wave: cooling centers and help
dek: Heat is hard on older bodies. Here is how to find a cooling center in your county, warning signs of heat stroke, and help with cooling costs.
keyFacts: Find open cooling centers by county at nj211.org/nj-cooling-centers, or dial 2-1-1
Heat stroke is an emergency: call 911
Fans alone may not help once indoor temperatures pass 90 degrees F (CDC)
Some medicines, including diuretics and certain heart and blood pressure drugs, reduce sweating
LIHEAP can help with cooling costs when there is a medical need: 1-800-510-3102
body:
New Jersey summers can turn dangerous fast. A few days of high heat and humidity can make an apartment without air conditioning hotter than it is outside. For older adults, that heat is more than uncomfortable. It can lead to heat stroke, which is a medical emergency.

This guide explains why heat hits older adults harder, how to find a cooling center in your county, what warning signs to watch for, and where to get help with cooling.

Why is heat harder on older adults?

The National Institutes of Health lists several reasons older people are at higher risk:

  • Age-related changes to the skin, such as poorer circulation and less efficient sweat glands.
  • Heart, lung or kidney disease, or any illness that causes weakness or fever.
  • High blood pressure, or conditions that require changes in diet, such as a low-salt diet.
  • Medicines that reduce sweating, including diuretics, sedatives, tranquilizers and certain heart and blood pressure drugs.
  • Being very overweight or underweight, drinking alcohol, or being dehydrated.
  • A very hot home, no transportation, or overdressing.

Do not stop a prescription because of the heat. NIH advises staying on your medicines and talking to your doctor about any worries. Ask your pharmacist at your next refill whether any of your medicines raise your heat risk.

How do I find a cooling center?

When the weather turns dangerous, counties and towns open cooling centers. These are often libraries, senior centers, community centers and other public buildings with air conditioning. Under the state's Code Red protocol, counties work with local emergency teams and social service agencies to provide cooling spots, water and sometimes transportation.

  1. Check NJ 211 online. The NJ 211 cooling centers list gathers information from state agencies, county emergency management offices and towns. Pick your county to see what is open.
  2. Or dial 2-1-1. NJ 211 can help you find what is open near you.
  3. Read the listing details. Each center sets its own hours and rules. Hours can change with local conditions.
  4. Check your town and county. NJ 211 suggests following your town and county social media accounts, which often post updates first.

If no centers show for your county, NJ 211 says that usually means it has not yet received updated information from local authorities. Call your town hall or your county office on aging. You can reach the county office through the Aging and Disability Resource Connection at 1-877-222-3737.

Air-conditioned public places like libraries, malls and movie theaters are also good places to spend the hottest hours, as NIH suggests.

Need a ride?

If you do not drive, ask when you call 2-1-1 or your county office whether transportation is available. Under Code Red, the state says counties may provide transportation when needed. Riders 62 and older also pay half fare on NJ Transit. See our NJ Transit senior fare guide.

What are the warning signs of heat stroke?

NIH lists these signs of heat stroke:

  • Body temperature over 104 degrees F
  • Fainting
  • Confusion, combative behavior, staggering or other changes in behavior
  • Dry, flushed skin and a strong, rapid pulse
  • Not sweating, even in the heat

The CDC also lists muscle cramps, heavy sweating, shortness of breath, dizziness, headache, weakness and nausea as signs your body is getting too hot.

What to do

If you think someone has heat stroke, call 911. While you wait, NIH advises:

  • Move the person to a cool, shaded or air-conditioned place and have them lie down.
  • If they can swallow safely, offer water or fruit or vegetable juice. No alcohol or caffeine.
  • Put cold, wet cloths on the wrists, neck, armpits and groin.
  • If it is safe, help them shower, bathe or sponge off with cool water.
Confusion on a hot day is not just old age. It can be heat stroke. Call 911.

How to stay cool at home

  • Stay inside on the hottest, most humid days, especially when there is an air quality alert.
  • Drink fluids through the day. The CDC suggests limiting sugary or salty drinks, caffeine and alcohol. If your doctor limits your fluids, ask what to do in a heat wave.
  • Wear light-colored, loose clothes made of natural fabrics.
  • Know the limits of fans. The CDC says to use fans only when indoor temperatures are below 90 degrees F. Above that, a fan can actually raise body temperature.
  • Do outdoor errands early or late. Garden or walk the dog in the cooler morning or evening.

Check on each other

The CDC urges people to check on family, friends and neighbors during heat, especially those who live alone or have chronic health problems. A daily phone call during a heat wave is a simple habit. If you are an adult child who lives far away, line up a neighbor who can knock on the door.

Help with cooling costs

New Jersey's Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program (LIHEAP) covers heating and cooling costs. The state says cooling help requires a medical need. For the current season, applications run October 1, 2026 to June 30, 2027, and the income limit for a one-person household is $51,273.

Apply online through the state's DCAid portal or with your local community action agency. Call 1-800-510-3102 to find where to apply. For more on energy help, see our food and utility help guide.

NIH also suggests contacting your local Area Agency on Aging or a senior center if cooling costs are a problem. In New Jersey, that is your county office on aging, reachable at 1-877-222-3737.

faq.a: Check the NJ 211 cooling centers list at nj211.org/nj-cooling-centers and choose your county, or dial 2-1-1. Each center sets its own hours, so read the listing before you go.

faq.q: What is a Code Red in New Jersey?
faq.a: Code Red is the state's emergency response when extreme heat or poor air quality becomes dangerous. Cooling centers open, and counties provide cooling locations, water and transportation when needed.

faq.q: What are the signs of heat stroke in older adults?
faq.a: A body temperature over 104 degrees F, fainting, confusion or other behavior changes, dry flushed skin with a strong rapid pulse, and not sweating. Call 911 right away.

faq.q: Is a fan enough during a heat wave?
faq.a: Not always. The CDC says to use fans only when indoor temperatures are below 90 degrees F. Above that, a fan can raise body temperature, so go somewhere air-conditioned.

faq.q: Can I get help paying for air conditioning in NJ?
faq.a: LIHEAP can help with cooling costs for eligible households that show a medical need. Call 1-800-510-3102 to find where to apply.

title: Holiday lights and events for older adults in New Jersey
dek: A handful of long-running New Jersey holiday traditions, from Cape May's candlelight tours to a free lights display in West Orange, with notes on walking, seating and tickets.
keyFacts: Dates for most 2026 events are posted in November; always check before you go
Cape May's Christmas Candlelight House Tour has run since 1974
Drumthwacket holiday open houses are free but need advance registration
McCarter's A Christmas Carol has a relaxed performance on December 26, 2026 at 3 p.m.
Ask about accessible parking, seating and walking distance when you book
body:
The holidays in New Jersey bring out lights on Victorian porches, carols in old theaters and a few traditions families return to every year. Many are easy to enjoy at any age, with a little planning around walking, parking and cold weather.

Below are some well-established events with official websites. Most groups post exact dates and prices in November, so treat this as a starting list. Always check the official site or call before you go.

Cape May: Victorian Christmas by the sea

Cape May MAC (Museums, Arts and Culture) runs a long holiday season of tours in the historic district. Its 2026 holiday tour list includes:

  • Christmas Candlelight House Tour. A self-guided evening walking tour of decorated homes, inns, B&Bs, churches and hotels. It has run since 1974.
  • Holiday Lights Trolley Ride. An evening guided trolley ride past decorated homes and streets. Cape May MAC notes the trolleys are open-air, so dress warmly.
  • Evening Yuletide House Tour. A 30-minute guided tour of the first floor of the 1879 Physick Estate, followed by the Carroll Gallery.
  • Holiday Inns House Tour and Lamplighter Christmas Tour. Daytime and evening self-guided tours of decorated properties.

Good to know: The house tours are walking tours, and historic homes may have steps. The trolley rides are the easier choice if walking is hard. Cape May MAC has an ADA accessibility page and offers tours for Deaf and hard of hearing visitors through its group tours office.

Details and tickets: capemaymac.org or 609-884-5404.

Storybook Land: Christmas Fantasy with Lights

This small amusement park in Egg Harbor Township near Atlantic City turns into a holiday show at dusk. The park says more than a million lights go on each operating night, and the event has been a family tradition for almost 40 years. It is a natural outing with grandchildren.

  • Tickets for the holiday event are sold online only, for a chosen date. They are not timed, so you can arrive any time that evening. Sales open October 28.
  • Visits with Santa run through December 23.
  • Senior pricing. The park lists discounts for seniors 65 and older. Ask whether it applies to holiday event tickets.
  • Access. The park offers an Assisted Access Pass for guests who have trouble waiting in standby lines, plus quiet zones. Call about wheelchair access and parking.

Details: storybookland.com or 609-646-0103. 6415 East Black Horse Pike, Egg Harbor Township.

Essex County Holiday Lights Spectacular, West Orange

Essex County puts on an annual holiday lights display at the Turtle Back Zoo and the surrounding South Mountain Recreation Complex in West Orange. In the 2025 season it ran from November into early January.

In recent years admission has been free. The county asks visitors to bring donations such as non-perishable food, toys or winter coats for people in need. Check the Essex County website for this year's dates and hours. Ask about parking and walking distance if you use a cane or wheelchair.

Princeton: Drumthwacket and McCarter Theatre

Drumthwacket holiday open houses

Drumthwacket, the official residence of New Jersey's governor, holds free holiday open houses on select days in December. You must register online in advance. In past years, sessions ran in one-hour blocks in late morning and early afternoon. The Drumthwacket Foundation says 2026 dates will be posted in early November.

Parking is free on site but limited. Small transit buses used by senior centers may park on site, so this is a good trip to suggest to your senior center. For questions about access, call 973-204-2860 or email info@drumthwacket.org. Details at drumthwacket.org.

A Christmas Carol at McCarter

McCarter Theatre Center in Princeton stages A Christmas Carol again in December 2026 at its Matthews Theatre. McCarter's accessibility services are worth knowing about:

  • A relaxed performance on December 26 at 3 p.m. Lights stay partly on, doors stay open and moving around is fine. It can be a good fit for a grandparent with memory loss, or anyone who may need to step out.
  • Free assistive listening headsets, with neck loops for T-coil hearing aids.
  • Wheelchair seating with companion seats, and large print programs.
  • Wider seats, with or without armrests, on request.
  • A limited number of accessible parking spaces at the Matthews Theatre for valid placards, first come, first served.

McCarter also offers ASL, audio description and open captioning at set performances of its theater series. Ask the box office which dates apply. Box office: 609-258-2787, Tuesday to Saturday, noon to 6 p.m. Details at mccarter.org/accessibility.

First Night Ocean City

Ocean City rings in the new year with First Night, now celebrating 34 years. On Thursday, December 31, 2026, it runs from 4 p.m. to midnight, with more than 70 events at over 20 venues. Admission is by button, sold online. The early evening shows are a good choice if you would rather be home well before midnight.

Details: firstnightocnj.com.

Check the date, call about access, then bundle up. That is most of the planning.

Closer to home

Some of the best holiday events are small and local. Look for:

  • Town tree lightings and menorah lightings, usually listed on your town's website.
  • Library concerts and craft afternoons. Libraries post winter calendars in November.
  • Senior center trips. Some centers run bus outings to light displays, which solves the night driving problem.
  • House of worship concerts, which are often free and warm.

Your county office on aging can tell you about local senior outings. Call the Aging and Disability Resource Connection at 1-877-222-3737.

Tips for a comfortable outing

  • Call ahead about access. Ask about accessible parking, how far you will walk, whether there are steps, where to sit and where the restrooms are.
  • Bring your placard. See our guide to NJ disability parking placards.
  • Dress in layers. Open-air trolleys and outdoor light shows get cold fast after dark.
  • Avoid night driving if it bothers you. Go with family, take a senior center bus, or ride NJ Transit at half fare. See NJ Transit senior fares.
  • Plan a rest stop. A warm cafe or a bench indoors makes a long evening easier.

For more winter ideas, see our winter in New Jersey guide, our grandkids day out guide and our off-season shore guide.

faq.a: They run on select evenings during the holiday season and have been held since 1974. Cape May MAC posts the exact dates and tickets on capemaymac.org, or call 609-884-5404.

faq.q: Is Storybook Land's Christmas lights event good for seniors?
faq.a: Many grandparents go with grandchildren. Tickets are bought online for a set date and are not timed. The park lists senior discounts for ages 65 and up and offers an Assisted Access Pass for guests who have trouble waiting in lines.

faq.q: Are the Drumthwacket holiday open houses free?
faq.a: Yes, but you must register online in advance and space is limited. The 2026 dates will be posted in early November on drumthwacket.org.

faq.q: Does McCarter's A Christmas Carol have accessible performances?
faq.a: Yes. There is a relaxed performance on December 26, 2026 at 3 p.m. McCarter also offers free assistive listening devices, wheelchair seating and large print programs. Call 609-258-2787.

faq.q: Is the Essex County Holiday Lights Spectacular free?
faq.a: In recent years admission has been free, with visitors asked to donate items such as food, toys or coats. Check the Essex County website for this year's dates.

title: Medicare Advantage or Medigap in NJ: how plans differ by county
dek: Medicare Advantage choices depend on the county you live in. Medigap mostly does not. Here is how to compare what is really available at your address, with free help from NJ SHIP.
keyFacts: Medicare Advantage plans are approved for set service areas, so choices differ by county
NJ SHIP's 2026 chart listed about 65 Advantage plans from 9 companies, many limited to certain counties
Medigap prices on NJ SHIP's age 65 chart are mostly the same statewide
Open Enrollment: October 15 to December 7, 2026; changes start January 1
Free NJ SHIP counseling in all 21 counties: 1-800-792-8820
body:
Two friends can both live in New Jersey and see very different Medicare Advantage choices. A retiree in Bergen County and one in Salem County may not have the same plans, the same networks or the same hospitals to choose from. That is because Advantage plans are sold by service area, which in New Jersey usually means by county.

Medigap works differently. This guide explains what changes from county to county, what does not, and how to compare plans at your own address. For the basics of each path, start with our Medicare Advantage vs. Medigap guide.

Medicare Open Enrollment runs October 15 to December 7, 2026. Changes take effect January 1, 2027.

Why do Medicare Advantage plans vary by county?

Each Medicare Advantage plan is approved for a specific service area. Insurers decide which counties to offer each plan in, and they build networks of doctors and hospitals there.

You can see this in NJ SHIP's chart of 2026 New Jersey Medicare Advantage plans, current as of October 28, 2025. It listed about 65 plans from nine companies. Some plans were offered in all 21 counties. Others were offered in a short list of counties, or in every county but one.

So the questions that matter are:

  • Which plans are offered in my county for 2027?
  • Which of those include my doctors and my hospital?
  • Do they cover my prescriptions at my pharmacy?

A plan a friend loves in another county may not be sold where you live. Even the same plan can have different nearby doctors in different counties.

Near a state line?

Many New Jersey residents get care in New York City or Philadelphia. If that is you, check whether each plan's network includes those doctors and hospitals. With Original Medicare and Medigap, you can see any doctor or hospital in the country that accepts Medicare.

Does Medigap cost more in some counties?

Mostly no, based on the state's own rate chart. NJ SHIP's September 2026 chart of Medigap premiums at age 65 lists 18 insurers. Almost all show a single statewide price for each plan letter. One company on that chart charged a different rate in certain Newark ZIP codes.

What does vary is the company and the plan letter. Prices for the same plan letter can be quite different from one insurer to the next. NJ SHIP also notes that rates can change during the year with approval from the NJ Department of Banking and Insurance, and that some companies offer household discounts. Always confirm the price with the company.

The bigger Medigap issue in New Jersey is timing. Your best chance to buy is the six-month Medigap Open Enrollment Period that starts when you are 65 and enrolled in Part B. After that, companies can ask health questions. Our Advantage vs. Medigap guide explains the rules, including New Jersey's coverage for people under 65 on Medicare due to disability.

How do I compare plans at my address?

Step 1: Use Medicare Plan Finder

  1. Go to Medicare Plan Finder on Medicare.gov. Enter your ZIP code.
  2. Enter your drugs, with the exact doses, and pick one or two pharmacies you use.
  3. Compare total yearly cost, not only the premium. Look at the drug costs, the deductible and the plan's yearly out-of-pocket limit.
  4. Check the star ratings and whether the plan is an HMO or a PPO.

Prefer the phone? Call 1-800-MEDICARE, 1-800-633-4227 (TTY 1-877-486-2048), any time, day or night, except some federal holidays.

Step 2: Call your doctors

Plan Finder cannot promise a doctor will stay in a network. Call each doctor's billing office and ask if they will be in network for the exact plan name for 2027.

Step 3: Get a free second opinion from NJ SHIP

The State Health Insurance Assistance Program (SHIP) gives free, unbiased Medicare counseling. Counselors do not sell anything and do not recommend specific products. They help you understand your options and compare plans. NJ SHIP also publishes the state's Medicare Advantage, Part D and Medigap rate charts.

Compare at your own ZIP code. A plan your friend has may not be sold where you live.

NJ SHIP counseling by county

SHIP counseling is available in all 21 counties. Call the statewide line at 1-800-792-8820 or your county's lead agency below. Call early in Open Enrollment if you can.

What if I move to another county?

If you move out of your Medicare Advantage plan's service area, you get a Special Enrollment Period. Medicare says your chance to switch starts when you move and lasts two full months after. If you tell your plan before you move, it can start the month before.

During that time you can join a new Advantage plan or drug plan, or go back to Original Medicare. If you do nothing, you will be put in Original Medicare when your old plan drops you. Moving out of a plan's area can also give you a guaranteed right to buy certain Medigap policies.

The same Special Enrollment Period applies if you move within your plan's area but have new plan options at your new address. This matters if a parent moves in with you, into senior housing in another county, or to the shore. See our housing options guide for more on moving.

Help paying for Medicare

If money is tight, ask SHIP about programs that lower Medicare and drug costs. New Jersey's PAAD and Senior Gold programs help with prescriptions, and some Advantage plans have lower premiums for people with PAAD, Medicaid or Extra Help. See our guide to prescription and bill help. New to Medicare? Start with Medicare at 65.

faq.a: Mostly no. On NJ SHIP's September 2026 chart for age 65, nearly every insurer listed one statewide price per plan. Prices do vary a lot between companies, so compare.

faq.a: Yes. NJ SHIP counseling is free and unbiased. Counselors do not sell insurance or recommend specific products. Help is available in all 21 counties.

title: Assisted living vs. home care in NJ: costs and how to choose
dek: Stay home with paid help, or move to assisted living? Here is what each costs in New Jersey, who pays, and the questions that usually decide it.
keyFacts: CareScout 2025: NJ non-medical home care median $38 an hour
At 44 hours a week, that is about $7,245 a month
CareScout 2025: NJ assisted living median $8,710 a month (private one-bedroom)
Medicare does not pay for long-term custodial care in either setting
NJ Medicaid MLTSS can cover both home services and assisted living for those who qualify
body:
Most families reach this question after a fall, a hospital stay or a run of small scares. Mom wants to stay in her house. You want her safe. Both are reasonable, and both cost real money in New Jersey.

This guide compares home care and assisted living on cost, care, safety and daily life, then walks through the questions that usually settle it.

What is the difference?

Home care means aides come to your parent's home. They can help with meals, housekeeping and errands. Certified aides can help with hands-on care like bathing, dressing and toileting. You pay by the hour, so the cost depends on how many hours you need.

Assisted living is a licensed residence where your parent has a private apartment or room. Meals, housekeeping, activities and help with daily tasks are built in, and staff are on site around the clock. You pay a monthly fee, and many residences charge more as care needs grow.

In New Jersey, assisted living residences are licensed by the NJ Department of Health. Home care companies that place aides must register with the NJ Division of Consumer Affairs. Our guide to choosing a home care agency explains how to check a license.

What does each cost in New Jersey?

The best regular source is CareScout's Cost of Care Survey, which has run since 2004 and was long published under the Genworth name. The 2025 survey collected prices from providers between July and November 2025.

CareScout 2025, New Jersey medianCost
Home care, non-medical caregiver$38 an hour
Home care at 44 hours a week$7,245 a month ($86,944 a year)
Assisted living, private one-bedroom$8,710 a month ($104,520 a year)
Adult day health care$100 a day

These are medians. Prices vary across the state and from one provider to the next, so get written quotes.

Doing the math

Home care is cheaper when your parent needs a few hours a day. At the median rate, 4 hours a day, 7 days a week is about $1,064 a week, or roughly $4,600 a month. That leaves room for nights alone.

Home care gets expensive as hours climb. At around 44 hours a week, it reaches $7,245 a month in CareScout's figures, and you still pay the mortgage or rent, taxes, food and utilities at home. Round-the-clock care at home costs much more than either.

Assisted living rolls housing, meals and some care into one bill. But read the fee sheet. Some residences charge a base rate plus extra for medication help, more care, or a second person.

Home care is priced by the hour. Assisted living is priced by the month. Compare them by the week your parent actually needs.

Who pays?

  • Medicare does not pay for long-term custodial care, at home or in assisted living. It can cover short-term home health visits from a nurse or therapist after an illness, when your parent is homebound and a doctor orders it.
  • NJ Medicaid's Managed Long Term Services and Supports (MLTSS) can pay for services at home, including care management, home-delivered meals and respite, and can also pay for assisted living. Your parent must meet financial rules and need a nursing home level of care. Ask each residence whether it accepts Medicaid. See our MLTSS guide.
  • Long-term care insurance, if your parent has it. Call the insurer early to learn what triggers benefits and whether there is a waiting period.
  • Veterans benefits. Ask your county veterans service office whether any VA benefits apply.
  • Private savings and home equity pay for most care in the end.

For a free screening for public programs, call the Aging and Disability Resource Connection at 1-877-222-3737.

How do we choose?

These questions often decide it:

How many hours of help are needed?

If your parent mainly needs help with meals, a shower a few times a week and company, home care often works. If they need help at night, wander, or cannot be alone, assisted living or full-time care is usually safer.

Is the house still safe?

Stairs to the only bathroom, a long driveway and icy steps all add risk. Grab bars, a stair lift or a first-floor bedroom can help. See our aging in place guide.

How lonely is your parent?

Isolation is a real health risk. Assisted living offers meals with others and activities on site. At home, adult day programs, senior centers and regular visitors can fill that gap. Our staying connected guide has ideas.

Who is backing up the plan?

Home care depends on aides showing up. When one calls out sick, someone has to fill in. If family lives far away, a residence with staff on site may bring more peace of mind.

What does your parent want?

This matters most. Ask, and listen. Our guide to the first conversation about care can help.

A middle path

Many families mix options. Adult day health care a few days a week, plus some aide hours, can keep a parent home longer for less than full-time care. It also gives family caregivers a break. See our respite care guide.

How to check an assisted living residence

  1. Confirm the license. Search the NJ Department of Health's facility search for nursing homes, assisted living and specialized care facilities.
  2. Visit more than once, including at a mealtime.
  3. Get the full fee sheet and the admission agreement in writing. Ask what happens to the price as needs increase.
  4. Ask about Medicaid. If savings may run out, ask whether your parent can stay once they switch to Medicaid.
  5. Ask about discharge. In New Jersey, assisted living residents have the right to written notice at least 30 days before a facility-requested transfer or discharge.

Complaints about a licensed facility go to the NJ Department of Health hotline at 1-800-792-9770, 24 hours a day. The Long-Term Care Ombudsman advocates for residents at 1-877-582-6995.

If you need a professional to assess your parent and lay out options, a geriatric care manager can help. For a fuller picture of prices, see what senior care costs in New Jersey.

faq.a: It depends on hours. CareScout's 2025 medians put NJ home care at $38 an hour and assisted living at $8,710 a month. Part-time home care is usually cheaper, but at around 44 hours a week home care reaches about $7,245 a month, before housing costs.

faq.a: No. Medicare does not pay for long-term custodial care, including assisted living. NJ Medicaid's MLTSS program can pay for assisted living for people who qualify, at residences that accept it.

faq.q: Does NJ Medicaid pay for home care?
faq.a: NJ Medicaid's MLTSS program covers services at home for people who meet financial rules and need a nursing home level of care. Call the ADRC at 1-877-222-3737 for a screening.

faq.q: How do I check if an assisted living facility is licensed in NJ?
faq.a: Use the NJ Department of Health facility search for nursing homes, assisted living and specialized care facilities. You can also file complaints with the Department at 1-800-792-9770.

faq.q: How much notice must NJ assisted living give before discharge?
faq.a: Residents have the right to written notice at least 30 days before a facility-requested transfer or discharge. The notice must include contact information for the Long-Term Care Ombudsman.

title: Nursing home vs. memory care in New Jersey
dek: When dementia makes home unsafe, families usually weigh a memory care unit against a nursing home. Here is how they differ, what each costs, who pays and how to check quality.
keyFacts: Memory care is usually a secure unit in assisted living; nursing homes provide 24-hour nursing
CareScout 2025: NJ nursing home median $12,775 a month semi-private, $14,448 private
Medicare covers up to 100 days of skilled nursing care per benefit period, not long-term custodial care
NJ Medicaid MLTSS can pay for assisted living or nursing home care for those who qualify
Check nursing homes on Medicare Care Compare and the NJ Department of Health facility search
body:
Dementia changes slowly, then sometimes all at once. A parent who managed at home with help may start wandering at night, forgetting to eat or getting lost on familiar roads. At that point, many families start looking at two kinds of places: memory care and nursing homes.

They can look similar on a tour. They are not the same. This guide explains the difference, what each costs in New Jersey, who pays, and how to check quality before you sign. For broader dementia help, see our dementia support guide.

What is the difference?

Memory care is usually a secure unit or wing within an assisted living residence. It is designed for people with Alzheimer's or another dementia who can still get around but need supervision, structure and help with daily tasks. Staff are there day and night, but residents generally do not need round-the-clock nursing.

A nursing home provides 24-hour nursing care. It suits people with serious medical needs, such as someone who cannot move without lifting help, has complex medications or wounds, or is near the end of life. Many nursing homes also have dementia units.

Memory care (assisted living)Nursing home
Best forDementia with mobility; needs supervision and daily helpDementia plus heavy medical or physical care needs
NursingStaff on site day and night; less nursing than a nursing home24-hour licensed nursing
SettingApartment or room in a secure unitUsually a semi-private or private room
Licensed byNJ Department of HealthNJ Department of Health
Medicare coverageNone for room, board or custodial careShort-term skilled care only, after a qualifying hospital stay

What does each cost in New Jersey?

CareScout's 2025 Cost of Care Survey gives these New Jersey medians:

CareScout 2025, NJ medianDailyMonthly
Nursing home, semi-private room$420$12,775
Nursing home, private room$475$14,448
Assisted living, private one-bedroom$286$8,710

CareScout does not publish a separate memory care figure. Memory care is priced by each residence and may cost more than regular assisted living. Ask for the memory care rate in writing, and ask what it includes.

Costs vary by region and by building, so these are a starting point, not a quote. See what senior care costs in New Jersey for more.

Who pays?

Medicare

Medicare does not pay for long-term custodial care. It can pay for a short stay in a skilled nursing facility after a hospital stay of at least three inpatient days, if your parent needs daily skilled nursing or therapy. In 2026, Medicare pays in full for days 1 to 20 after the Part A deductible, then your parent pays $217 a day for days 21 to 100. After day 100, Medicare pays nothing. Our hospital discharge guide explains these rules.

Medicaid

NJ Medicaid's Managed Long Term Services and Supports (MLTSS) program can pay for nursing home care or assisted living, including memory care units at residences that accept it. Your parent must meet financial rules and need a nursing home level of care. The state describes that as needing hands-on help with three or more activities of daily living, or having cognitive problems that require supervision and cueing for three or more. See our MLTSS guide.

Private pay

Most families pay privately at first. If your parent may run out of money, ask before moving in whether they can stay once Medicaid pays. An elder law attorney can explain planning options.

Before you sign, ask one question: can my parent stay here if the money runs out?

How do I judge a memory care unit?

New Jersey rules require assisted living residences that advertise an Alzheimer's or dementia program to provide a written list of activities designed for residents with dementia and how often they happen. The list must also describe safety policies and any security monitoring for those residents. Ask to see it.

Then look for yourself:

  • How are doors secured, and how do staff handle a resident who tries to leave?
  • How many staff are on the unit during the day and at night? The state requires residences with a dementia program to keep daily records of direct care staff on each shift.
  • What dementia training do aides have?
  • What happens if your parent's needs grow? When would they have to move to a nursing home?
  • Are residents up, dressed and engaged when you visit unannounced?

How do I check a nursing home?

  1. Look it up on Medicare Care Compare. Medicare's Five-Star Quality Rating System gives each nursing home an overall rating plus separate ratings for health inspections, staffing and quality measures. Find it on Medicare Care Compare.
  2. Read the stars with care. CMS itself says no rating covers everything. A nearby home where family can visit often may serve your parent better than a higher-rated one far away.
  3. Check the license and inspections through the NJ Department of Health facility search.
  4. Visit at different times, including evenings and weekends.
  5. Ask about the dementia unit, if there is one, and how they handle behaviors without overusing medication.

Where to get help

The NJ Long-Term Care Ombudsman advocates for residents of nursing homes and assisted living, including memory care. Call 1-877-582-6995 with questions or concerns. Complaints about care at a licensed facility can also go to the NJ Department of Health hotline at 1-800-792-9770, 24 hours a day. If you ever suspect abuse, see our guide to reporting elder abuse in New Jersey.

For a professional assessment and a short list of good options, a geriatric care manager can help. For a free screening for public programs, call the Aging and Disability Resource Connection at 1-877-222-3737.

faq.q: What is the difference between memory care and a nursing home?
faq.a: Memory care is usually a secure unit within assisted living for people with dementia who need supervision and daily help. A nursing home provides 24-hour licensed nursing for people with heavier medical or physical needs.

faq.q: How much does a nursing home cost in New Jersey?
faq.a: CareScout's 2025 survey put the New Jersey median at $12,775 a month for a semi-private room and $14,448 for a private room. Prices vary by region and facility.

faq.q: Does Medicare pay for memory care?
faq.a: No. Medicare does not pay for long-term custodial care, including memory care. It covers short skilled nursing stays after a qualifying hospital stay, up to 100 days per benefit period.

faq.q: Does NJ Medicaid pay for memory care?
faq.a: NJ Medicaid's MLTSS program can pay for assisted living, including memory care, at residences that accept Medicaid, for people who meet financial and clinical rules. Ask each residence whether it accepts Medicaid.

faq.q: How can I check a New Jersey nursing home's quality?
faq.a: Look it up on Medicare Care Compare for star ratings on inspections, staffing and quality measures. Check the license and inspection reports through the NJ Department of Health, and visit more than once.
